title: Fabrikam Manufacturing Analytics
scenario: Fabrikam Industries is a global manufacturing company with 12,000 employees across 8 sales regions. Their BI team built a Power BI solution three years ago that has become the primary reporting tool for regional sales managers and the executive team.
currentSetup: The model uses a single denormalized fact table SalesActivity (18.5 million rows, 52 columns) in DirectQuery mode against an on-premises SQL Server 2019. All KPI calculations — Revenue, GrossMargin, YTD_Revenue, YTD_Margin, and QoQ_Growth — are implemented as calculated columns. All model relationships use bidirectional cross-filter. RLS is configured with a 'Region Manager' role: [SalesRegion] = LOOKUPVALUE(RegionAccess[Region], RegionAccess[ManagerEmail], USERPRINCIPALNAME()). Average report load time: 11–14 seconds.
requirements: Reduce report load time to under 3 seconds without losing historical data access
Ensure regional managers see only data for their assigned region — the current implementation has intermittent security gaps
CFO requires a rolling 12-month revenue trend compared to the prior year on a monthly basis
Reports must be accessible to 250 internal Pro-licensed users and 20 external distributors without Power BI licenses

questions.question: Performance Analyzer shows YTD_Revenue and YTD_Margin calculated columns account for 9 of the 12 seconds of average load time. These columns are defined on the 18.5M-row SalesActivity table in DirectQuery mode. What is the MOST effective resolution?
choices: Convert SalesActivity to Import mode and rewrite YTD_Revenue and YTD_Margin as DAX time intelligence measures using DATESYTD
Add non-clustered indexes to the YTD and Margin columns in SQL Server to reduce formula engine computation
Reduce the slicer date range to 24 months using a report-level filter to limit the rows processed
Switch to DirectLake storage mode, which handles aggregation columns more efficiently than DirectQuery
questions.explanation: Calculated columns in DirectQuery mode are computed by the Formula Engine on every query — they are not stored in VertiPaq. With 18.5M rows, each YTD calculation iterates the full row set per visual refresh. Converting to Import mode stores data in compressed columnar storage, and rewriting as measures (evaluated on aggregated results at query time) reduces Formula Engine overhead by orders of magnitude. DirectLake requires OneLake/Fabric and cannot connect to on-premises SQL Server.

questions.question: Regional managers intermittently see sales data from other regions. The RLS filter on SalesActivity is: [SalesRegion] = LOOKUPVALUE(RegionAccess[Region], RegionAccess[ManagerEmail], USERPRINCIPALNAME()). RegionAccess is a standalone table with no model relationships. The issue affects some managers but not others. What is the MOST likely cause?
choices: LOOKUPVALUE returns BLANK when the manager's email is not found in RegionAccess — the expression [SalesRegion] = BLANK() then returns TRUE for rows where SalesRegion is null or empty, exposing those rows to unmatched managers
USERPRINCIPALNAME() returns different values in Power BI Desktop versus the Power BI Service, causing some managers to bypass the filter
The RegionAccess table must have a model relationship to SalesActivity for LOOKUPVALUE to evaluate correctly
The RLS filter should use USERNAME() instead of USERPRINCIPALNAME() when the source is an on-premises database
questions.explanation: This is a critical RLS security trap. When LOOKUPVALUE finds no matching email, it returns BLANK. The expression [SalesRegion] = BLANK() evaluates to TRUE for any row where SalesRegion is empty or null — inadvertently exposing those rows to every manager whose email is absent from RegionAccess. The 'intermittent' pattern (some managers affected, others not) is explained by which managers' emails are missing. The fix: IF(ISBLANK(LOOKUPVALUE(...)), FALSE(), [SalesRegion] = LOOKUPVALUE(...)).

questions.question: Fabrikam needs to distribute the regional sales report to 20 external distributors who do not have Power BI Pro licenses. The report contains commercially sensitive pricing data and distributors must not be able to export or download the underlying data. What is the MOST appropriate approach?
choices: Publish the report to a Premium capacity workspace and distribute via a Power BI App to external Azure AD B2B guest accounts — configure Export and sharing restrictions in workspace settings
Export the report as a PDF and send it via encrypted email on a monthly basis
Assign the external distributors Viewer roles on the workspace and issue them free Fabric (free tier) licenses
Publish the report with anonymous public access enabled and restrict access at the corporate network level
questions.explanation: Power BI Premium capacity allows external Azure AD B2B guest users to consume reports without per-user Pro licenses — the capacity license covers consumption. Distributing via a Power BI App provides controlled access, and Export restrictions can be enforced at workspace and tenant level. Viewer workspace roles (C) require Pro licenses in non-Premium workspaces. Anonymous access (D) bypasses all identity-based security controls. PDF export (B) is not a scalable operational solution.

recommendedSolutions.title: Rolling 12-Month Revenue Trend vs Prior Year
recommendedSolutions.overview: Create time intelligence DAX measures using SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR and display them in a matrix visual with months on rows. A marked, contiguous DimDate table is a prerequisite.

steps.label: Mark the Date Table
steps.detail: In Power BI Desktop, select DimDate → Table Tools → Mark as Date Table, setting the Date column as the date key. Verify the date range covers all historical data with no gaps.

steps.label: Create the prior-year measure
steps.detail:
Revenue LY = CALCULATE([Revenue], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(DimDate[Date]))

This shifts the current date filter context back exactly 12 months. When the report shows Jan 2024, [Revenue LY] returns Jan 2023 data.

steps.label: Create the YoY % change measure
steps.detail:
YoY % Change = DIVIDE([Revenue] - [Revenue LY], [Revenue LY])

DIVIDE handles the divide-by-zero case where [Revenue LY] is BLANK for the earliest periods.

steps.label: Build the CFO visual
steps.detail: Place a Matrix visual on the CFO page. Set Rows = DimDate[Year-Month] (formatted "MMM YYYY"), Values = [Revenue], [Revenue LY], [YoY % Change]. Apply a relative date filter to the last 13 months to show 12 complete months plus the current partial month.

steps.label: Add conditional formatting
steps.detail: Apply conditional formatting to [YoY % Change] — green background for positive %, red for negative. This makes the monthly trend immediately readable without needing to read raw numbers.

recommendedSolutions.daxCode:
-- Step 1: Prior year revenue
Revenue LY =
CALCULATE(
    [Revenue],
    SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(DimDate[Date])
)

-- Step 2: Year-over-year % change
YoY % Change =
DIVIDE(
    [Revenue] - [Revenue LY],
    [Revenue LY]
)
recommendedSolutions.examNote: SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR requires a marked Date Table with no gaps. If the date table ends before the current year, it returns BLANK for recent periods. Always extend the date table to Dec 31 of the current or next year.

title: Northwind Financial Services Dashboard
scenario: Northwind Financial Services is a mid-sized investment management firm managing portfolios for 2,400 clients. The BI team is building a consolidated performance dashboard to replace manual Excel-based monthly reporting compiled from three separate source systems.
currentSetup: Data sources: (1) Azure SQL Database — client portfolio and transaction data, updated every 15 minutes. (2) SharePoint Online — weekly risk assessment Excel files uploaded by senior analysts. (3) On-premises SQL Server 2016 — legacy trade execution system, read-only BI access via data gateway, updated daily via overnight batch. Finance analysts currently export from all three sources, join in Excel, and email reports monthly. All data is subject to MiFID II compliance — client data must be labelled, audited, and access-controlled.
requirements: Automate data refresh — portfolio data must reflect changes within 2 hours; risk assessments and trade data may refresh daily
Senior analysts see all client data; junior analysts see only the portfolios assigned to them
All reports containing client data must carry the 'Highly Confidential' sensitivity label automatically
The solution must allow the BI team to manage access without IT involvement for routine access changes

questions.subtopic: Choose between DirectLake, DirectQuery, and Import
questions.question: Northwind must combine data from Azure SQL Database (updates every 15 minutes), SharePoint Excel (weekly), and on-premises SQL Server (daily batch via gateway). Portfolio data must reflect changes within 2 hours. Which combination of storage modes is MOST appropriate?
choices: Composite model — Import mode for SharePoint and on-premises SQL Server (scheduled daily refresh via on-premises gateway), DirectQuery for Azure SQL Database for near-real-time portfolio data
Full Import mode for all three sources with a 2-hour scheduled refresh cycle applied to the entire model
DirectQuery for all three sources to eliminate scheduled refresh dependency and ensure real-time access
DirectLake for Azure SQL Database and Import mode for the remaining sources — DirectLake provides sub-minute latency for Azure-hosted data
questions.explanation: A composite model allows each table to use the most appropriate storage mode. Azure SQL (frequent updates) benefits from DirectQuery — always current without refresh overhead. SharePoint Excel (weekly) and on-premises SQL (daily batch) are stable enough for scheduled Import refresh via the on-premises data gateway. Full Import with 2-hour refresh (B) continuously stresses all three source systems. DirectLake (D) requires Microsoft Fabric/OneLake and cannot connect to arbitrary external databases or on-premises systems.

questions.question: Junior analysts must see only client portfolios assigned to them. The model includes a ClientPortfolio fact table (ClientID, Revenue, RiskScore) and a separate PortfolioAssignment mapping table (AnalystUPN, ClientID) with no model relationship. Which RLS DAX filter applied to ClientPortfolio CORRECTLY restricts junior analysts to their assigned clients?
choices: [ClientID] IN SELECTCOLUMNS(FILTER(PortfolioAssignment, [AnalystUPN] = USERPRINCIPALNAME()), "CID", [ClientID])
USERPRINCIPALNAME() = [AnalystUPN]
[ClientID] = LOOKUPVALUE(PortfolioAssignment[ClientID], PortfolioAssignment[AnalystUPN], USERPRINCIPALNAME())
CALCULATE(COUNTROWS(FILTER(PortfolioAssignment, [AnalystUPN] = USERPRINCIPALNAME() && [ClientID] = EARLIER([ClientID])))) > 0
questions.explanation: The IN SELECTCOLUMNS(FILTER(...)) pattern correctly handles multi-value RLS from a disconnected mapping table — it returns the full set of ClientIDs assigned to the current user and filters ClientPortfolio to only those rows. LOOKUPVALUE (C) returns only the FIRST matching ClientID, so analysts managing multiple portfolios would see only one. Option B applies to the wrong table — ClientPortfolio has no AnalystUPN column. Option D uses EARLIER which is only valid inside calculated columns, not in RLS filter expressions.
questions.trapType: RLS LOOKUPVALUE vs IN for multiple rows

questions.question: Northwind's compliance requirement states all reports containing client financial data must carry the 'Highly Confidential' label. An analyst publishes a new report without applying the label. What is the MOST automated and scalable enforcement approach?
choices: Configure mandatory sensitivity label policies in Microsoft Purview that set 'Highly Confidential' as the default label for Power BI content in the workspace and prevent saving without a label
Instruct all workspace Admins to manually review and apply labels to newly published content within 24 hours of publication
Enable downstream sensitivity label inheritance — reports automatically inherit the label from their source semantic model when the model carries 'Highly Confidential'
Restrict publishing rights to workspace Admins only, who verify labels are applied before publishing on behalf of analysts
questions.explanation: Downstream label inheritance (C) is the most automated approach for this scenario. When the source semantic model is labelled 'Highly Confidential', all reports built from it automatically inherit that label — no analyst action required. This is the standard Power BI + Purview integration pattern. Mandatory Purview policies (A) are the strongest enforcement control but require additional compliance licensing and admin configuration. Manual admin review (B, D) introduces human error and does not scale to a BI team publishing frequently.

recommendedSolutions.title: Self-Service Access Management via Power BI Apps
recommendedSolutions.overview: Create a Power BI App from the workspace with audience groups. Workspace Admins (the BI team) can add or remove users from app audiences at any time without IT involvement — no Azure AD group changes or IT tickets required.

steps.label: Configure workspace roles for the BI team
steps.detail: Assign BI team members the Admin or Member workspace role. This allows them to manage app audiences and workspace permissions independently of IT.

steps.label: Create the Power BI App
steps.detail: In the workspace, select Create app. Configure the App name, description, and navigation. The App is the distribution vehicle — workspace content is not shared directly.

steps.label: Define App audiences
steps.detail: Create two audiences: "Senior Analysts" (access to all reports) and "Junior Analysts" (access to portfolio-level reports only). Each audience can be mapped to different report tabs and permission levels.

steps.label: Assign users to audiences
steps.detail: In the App Permissions section, add individual user emails or Azure AD security groups to each audience. The BI team can update this list directly in Power BI Service at any time — no IT support needed for routine changes like onboarding new analysts.

steps.label: Connect App audiences to RLS roles
steps.detail: In the semantic model Security settings, assign the same user lists to the corresponding RLS roles (Senior Analyst role = no filter, Junior Analyst role = portfolio assignment filter). When users change, update both the App audience and the RLS role assignment.

recommendedSolutions.examNote: Power BI App audiences control which content users see in the App. Workspace roles control what operations users can perform on workspace items. RLS controls which data rows users can see. These are three distinct, complementary permission layers.

title: Contoso Healthcare Patient Analytics
scenario: Contoso Regional Health System operates 6 hospitals and 40 outpatient clinics across three states. Their analytics team is building a centralized Power BI solution to consolidate patient outcome metrics, operational throughput, and financial performance for clinical and administrative leaders.
currentSetup: Data is stored in an Azure Synapse Analytics dedicated SQL pool (patient encounters, procedures, billing — 220 million rows). Clinical reference data (ICD codes, provider rosters, facility mappings) is maintained in Excel workbooks on SharePoint. Refresh: the Synapse pool receives daily batch loads at 2:00 AM. All patient-identifiable information is classified as Protected Health Information (PHI) under HIPAA. Department heads should only see data for patients within their department. The executive team requires an enterprise-wide view. Current report build times in Power BI Desktop range from 45 seconds to 3 minutes per visual when connected via DirectQuery.
requirements: Patient-level data must never be exposed to unauthorized users — department heads see only their department
Report performance must allow executives to load a 6-hospital summary in under 5 seconds
Source data changes daily — reports must reflect yesterday's data by 6:00 AM
PHI fields must be masked or excluded from any export functionality

questions.subtopic: Choose between DirectLake, DirectQuery, and Import
questions.question: The analytics team is evaluating storage modes for the 220M-row patient encounters table in Synapse Analytics. Executives report 45-second visual load times in DirectQuery mode. Refresh must reflect yesterday's data by 6:00 AM. Which storage mode configuration BEST meets both the performance and freshness requirements?
choices: Import mode with incremental refresh policy — partition by EncounterDate, import only the last 3 days on each refresh cycle, retain 5 years historical in frozen partitions, schedule refresh at 3:00 AM
DirectQuery mode with Synapse materialized views pre-aggregating the most common executive KPIs to eliminate Formula Engine overhead
DirectLake mode pointing to the Synapse-backed OneLake delta tables for zero-ETL import with automatic framing at each batch load
Composite model — DirectQuery for the current month's encounters for live data, Import for all prior months
questions.explanation: Import mode with incremental refresh is the standard PL-300 answer for large tables with daily batch loads and sub-second performance requirements. Incremental refresh partitions the table so only recent data is re-imported each cycle (here 3 days covers batch delays), while historical partitions remain frozen — avoiding a full 220M-row import daily. VertiPaq compression on Import mode delivers the sub-5-second executive load times. DirectQuery with materialized views (B) reduces load but cannot match Import compression ratios at 220M rows. DirectLake (C) requires Microsoft Fabric; Synapse dedicated SQL pools do not automatically expose OneLake delta tables without Fabric integration.

questions.question: The model has a DimDepartment table with a DepartmentHead_UPN column. Department heads must see only encounters where Encounter[DepartmentID] matches their assigned department. Executives belong to an 'Executive' Azure AD security group and must bypass department filtering. Which RLS design CORRECTLY implements this without creating separate roles for each department?
choices: Create a single 'DeptHead' role with filter on DimDepartment: [DepartmentHead_UPN] = USERPRINCIPALNAME(). Add executives to a separate 'Executive' role with no filter. Assign users to exactly one role in the semantic model.

Create a 'DeptHead' role with filter on the Encounter fact table: [DepartmentID] IN VALUES(DimDepartment[DepartmentID]). Use LOOKUPVALUE to retrieve the department of the current user from a separate HR table.
Create one role with the DAX filter: IF(USERPRINCIPALNAME() IN VALUES(ExecRoster[UPN]), TRUE(), [DepartmentHead_UPN] = USERPRINCIPALNAME()). Apply the filter to DimDepartment.
Create a dynamic role using USERNAME() on the Encounter table: [DepartmentID] = LOOKUPVALUE(DimDepartment[DepartmentID], DimDepartment[DepartmentHead_UPN], USERNAME())
questions.explanation: The correct pattern uses separate named roles — one for department heads filtered via DimDepartment (which propagates to Encounter via the relationship), and one for executives with no filter. Power BI applies the most permissive role when a user belongs to multiple roles, so executives assigned to the 'Executive' role see all data. This avoids the maintenance burden of per-department roles. Option C places the executive check inside a DAX IF expression — this pattern is not reliably supported in Power BI RLS and can produce unexpected results. Option D uses USERNAME() which returns domain\user format on-premises, not UPN — unreliable in the Power BI Service.

questions.question: HIPAA compliance requires that PHI fields (PatientName, DateOfBirth, SSN_Last4) must never be exportable from Power BI reports, even by department heads who can view them on screen. The fields are visible in table and matrix visuals for clinical users. What is the MOST appropriate configuration?
choices: In the Power BI Admin portal, disable 'Export data' for the workspace under tenant settings; supplement with sensitivity labels that restrict export on the semantic model

Remove PatientName, DateOfBirth, and SSN_Last4 from all visuals and replace with a de-identified PatientToken column; retain PHI only in a separate restricted semantic model used by authorized clinical apps
Set the semantic model sensitivity label to 'Highly Confidential — PHI' in Microsoft Purview and configure label-based protection to block download/export actions
Configure workspace-level export restrictions to 'Allow export with restrictions' and instruct report authors to exclude PHI columns from table visuals
questions.explanation: The only reliable way to prevent PHI export is to exclude it from the model entirely for general reporting. If PHI is present in the semantic model, any user with Build permission or data export capability could access it regardless of visual-level hiding. De-identification at the model level (B) is the architecturally sound HIPAA-compliant approach — clinical detail is served through a separate, purpose-built restricted model. Sensitivity labels (C) add a governance layer but rely on Microsoft 365 label enforcement, which does not prevent all export paths. Admin portal export restrictions (A, D) are policy controls that can be bypassed by users with the right permissions or desktop tools.

recommendedSolutions.title: Scheduled Incremental Refresh for 6 AM Data Currency
recommendedSolutions.overview: The storage mode decision (Import + incremental refresh) is covered by Q1. This solution details the scheduling configuration needed to guarantee yesterday data is available by 6:00 AM.

steps.label: Define the incremental refresh policy in Desktop
steps.detail: Select the FactEncounters table, open incremental refresh settings. Set: Store rows from last 3 years (frozen historical partitions), Refresh rows from last 3 days (rolling incremental window). This ensures nightly batch data lands in the refresh window without re-importing all 220M rows.

steps.label: Schedule the refresh at 3:00 AM
steps.detail: In Power BI Service, navigate to the semantic model settings, then Scheduled refresh. Set a daily refresh at 3:00 AM — the Synapse batch load completes by 2:30 AM. The incremental-only refresh finishes in 10-20 minutes, making data available well before 6:00 AM.

steps.label: Enable refresh failure notifications
steps.detail: In the semantic model settings, enable email notifications on refresh failure. Designate the BI lead as the contact so a pre-6 AM failure triggers an immediate alert before clinical users arrive at shift start.

recommendedSolutions.examNote: Incremental refresh policy is defined in Desktop (Power Query parameters + partition rules) and scheduled in the Service. Historical partitions are frozen and skipped on each refresh cycle — only the rolling window partition is re-queried.

title: Adventure Works Retail Modernization
scenario: Adventure Works is a sporting goods retailer with 180 stores across North America, a growing e-commerce channel, and a wholesale distribution arm. Their BI team is migrating from SSRS paginated reports to an interactive Power BI solution serving 600 store managers, 15 regional directors, and the executive board.
currentSetup: Source: on-premises SQL Server 2019 data warehouse with a partially normalized star schema. The FactSales table has 95 million rows. DimCustomer has a Type 2 SCD (historical rows with IsCurrent flag). The team currently runs 3 separate SQL queries to produce a monthly P&L: one for store sales, one for e-commerce, and one for wholesale. Each query returns different grain (store/day, order/hour, invoice/month). Marketing wants a DAX measure that shows 'Sales vs Same Period Last Year' with the ability to slice by store, product category, and channel.
requirements: Unify store, e-commerce, and wholesale sales into a single fact table at day-channel-store grain without losing order-level e-commerce detail
The SCD Type 2 DimCustomer must correctly attribute sales to the customer profile active at the time of sale
The 'Sales vs Same Period Last Year' measure must work correctly with any combination of date, store, category, and channel slicers
Regional directors must see all stores in their region; store managers see only their own store

questions.question: The team needs to combine store sales (day-store grain), e-commerce orders (hourly), and wholesale invoices (monthly) into a single FactSales table. Store and e-commerce data share the same SalesDate, StoreID, ProductID, and Revenue columns. Wholesale invoices have InvoiceDate, DistributorID, ProductID, and InvoiceRevenue with no StoreID. Which Power Query approach BEST supports a unified model without distorting granularity?
choices: Append store and e-commerce queries (matching columns), add a Channel column to each before appending; load wholesale as a separate FactWholesale table linked to a shared DimProduct and DimDate — avoid forcing into FactSales due to grain mismatch
Merge all three queries using a full outer join on ProductID and date, filling nulls for missing columns with 0 to ensure no rows are dropped
Append all three sources and add a grain identifier column; aggregate to day-store grain using Group By on SalesDate and StoreID before loading
Create a reference query from FactSales, filter by Channel, and use Merge to add wholesale data via a left outer join on ProductID
questions.explanation: When combining datasets with different grains, forcing them into the same fact table introduces data integrity risks. Appending store and e-commerce (same day-store grain) is valid. Wholesale at invoice-month grain with no StoreID cannot be cleanly appended — DistributorID does not map to StoreID, and aggregating to day would fabricate sub-invoice data. A separate FactWholesale table sharing DimProduct and DimDate allows accurate analysis at each table's natural grain. A full outer join (B) on ProductID alone is meaningless — one product can have millions of sales rows. Forced aggregation (C) loses the e-commerce hourly detail that was specified as a requirement.

questions.subtopic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.question: The marketing team wants a measure [Sales vs SPLY %] that compares current period sales to the same period last year, working correctly with any combination of date, store, product category, and channel slicers. The model has a standard DimDate table marked as a date table with a DateKey column. Which DAX measure is MOST correct?
choices: Sales vs SPLY % = DIVIDE([Total Sales] - CALCULATE([Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(DimDate[Date])), CALCULATE([Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(DimDate[Date])))
Sales vs SPLY % = DIVIDE([Total Sales] - CALCULATE([Total Sales], DATEADD(DimDate[Date], -1, YEAR)), CALCULATE([Total Sales], DATEADD(DimDate[Date], -1, YEAR)))
Sales vs SPLY % = DIVIDE([Total Sales], CALCULATE([Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(DimDate[Date]))) - 1
Sales vs SPLY % = ([Total Sales] - [Total Sales LY]) / [Total Sales LY]
questions.explanation: Option C is the most concise and correct form: DIVIDE(Current, PY) - 1 gives the percentage change. SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR respects the current date filter context from all slicers (date, store, category, channel) and is the standard PL-300 time intelligence function for this pattern. Option A is logically equivalent but unnecessarily calculates SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR twice (no variable reuse). Option B using DATEADD -1 YEAR is functionally similar but SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR is preferred for this exact use case. Option D references [Total Sales LY] as if it were a separate named measure — if that measure is undefined, the formula breaks; this pattern should be self-contained or use VAR.

questions.question: FactSales has two date foreign keys: OrderDate and ShipDate. Both need to relate to DimDate for time intelligence. The team creates two relationships between FactSales and DimDate, but Power BI only allows one to be active. A measure [Sales by Ship Date] must correctly use the ShipDate relationship for SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR. How should this be implemented?
choices: Keep the OrderDate → DimDate relationship active. Create [Sales by Ship Date] using CALCULATE([Total Sales], USERELATIONSHIP(FactSales[ShipDate], DimDate[DateKey])). Wrap the SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR call inside the same CALCULATE.
Create a second copy of DimDate named DimShipDate and establish a separate active relationship from FactSales[ShipDate] to DimShipDate[DateKey]
Mark both relationships as active — Power BI will use the relationship that matches the slicer's connected date dimension
Add a ShipYear, ShipMonth calculated column to FactSales using RELATED(DimDate[Year]) to avoid needing a second relationship
questions.explanation: Role-playing dimensions are handled in Power BI by keeping one relationship active and activating the inactive relationship within a CALCULATE using USERELATIONSHIP. The SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR function must be inside the same CALCULATE that activates the USERELATIONSHIP — both modifiers apply within that filter context scope. A duplicate DimDate table (B) is the alternative approach and works correctly, but USERELATIONSHIP is the preferred PL-300 pattern when a single dimension serves multiple roles. Power BI does not allow two active relationships between the same tables (C is invalid). Calculated columns via RELATED (D) would return the OrderDate dimension values, not ShipDate.

recommendedSolutions.title: SCD Type 2 — Attributing Sales to the Active Customer Profile
recommendedSolutions.overview: Connect FactSales to DimCustomer using the customer surrogate key active at the time of sale — not the current customer key. This ensures historical sales are attributed to the correct profile version even after the customer record changes.

steps.label: Understand the SCD Type 2 key structure
steps.detail: In a Type 2 SCD, each historical version of a customer record gets a unique surrogate key (e.g., CustomerSK). The IsCurrent = TRUE row is the active record. The CustomerID (natural key) repeats across versions but CustomerSK is unique per version.

steps.label: Add CustomerSK to FactSales during ETL
steps.detail: During ETL, join the source orders table to DimCustomer on CustomerID WHERE OrderDate BETWEEN StartDate AND EndDate (or WHERE IsCurrent = TRUE at order time). Store the resulting CustomerSK in FactSales — this permanently records which version of the customer was active when the order was placed.

steps.label: Build the relationship on the surrogate key
steps.detail: Create the relationship: FactSales[CustomerSK] → DimCustomer[CustomerSK] (many-to-one). This connects each order to the exact customer version active at sale time, not the current record.

steps.label: Create a current-customer dimension (optional)
steps.detail: For visuals that need current customer attributes (e.g., current mailing address), create a DimCustomerCurrent calculated table: DimCustomerCurrent = FILTER(DimCustomer, DimCustomer[IsCurrent] = TRUE()). Connect this to FactSales via a separate inactive relationship for use with USERELATIONSHIP.

steps.label: Validate historical attribution
steps.detail: Test: find a customer who changed region in the last year. Their orders before the change should show the old region; orders after should show the new region. If both show the same region, the surrogate key join is not working correctly.

recommendedSolutions.examNote: The key PL-300 insight: in SCD Type 2, the relationship between fact and dimension must use the SURROGATE key (unique per version), not the natural/business key (which repeats across versions). Using the natural key means all historical orders always reflect the current customer state — defeating the purpose of Type 2.

recommendedSolutions.title: Hierarchical RLS — Store Managers and Regional Directors
recommendedSolutions.overview: Create two dynamic RLS roles using USERPRINCIPALNAME(): one filtering to a single store, one filtering to all stores in a region. A StoreAccess mapping table controls which stores/regions each user can see.

steps.label: Create the StoreAccess mapping table
steps.detail: Import a StoreAccess table with columns: UserEmail, StoreID, RegionID, Role ('Manager' or 'Director'). Each store manager has one row; each regional director has one row per store in their region (or one row with RegionID and a null StoreID).

steps.label: Create the StoreManager RLS role
steps.detail:
In Manage Roles, create role "StoreManager". Apply this DAX filter to DimStore:

[StoreID] IN
  SELECTCOLUMNS(
    FILTER(StoreAccess,
      [UserEmail] = USERPRINCIPALNAME()
      && [Role] = "Manager"
    ),
    "SID", [StoreID]
  )

This restricts the user to their single assigned store.

steps.label: Create the RegionalDirector RLS role
steps.detail:
Create role "RegionalDirector". Apply this filter to DimStore:

[RegionID] IN
  SELECTCOLUMNS(
    FILTER(StoreAccess,
      [UserEmail] = USERPRINCIPALNAME()
      && [Role] = "Director"
    ),
    "RID", [RegionID]
  )

The filter propagates from DimStore through the relationship to FactSales.

steps.label: Handle the LOOKUPVALUE BLANK risk
steps.detail: If a user's email is not in StoreAccess, the FILTER returns an empty table and IN returns FALSE — the user sees no data. This is safer than the LOOKUPVALUE = BLANK() vulnerability. Verify by testing with a user email not in the mapping table.

steps.label: Assign users to roles in Power BI Service
steps.detail: In the semantic model Security settings, add store managers to "StoreManager" and regional directors to "RegionalDirector". Test using View As Role for each user type before going live.

recommendedSolutions.daxCode:
-- StoreManager role filter on DimStore
[StoreID] IN
  SELECTCOLUMNS(
    FILTER(StoreAccess,
      [UserEmail] = USERPRINCIPALNAME()
      && [Role] = "Manager"
    ),
    "SID", [StoreID]
  )

-- RegionalDirector role filter on DimStore
[RegionID] IN
  SELECTCOLUMNS(
    FILTER(StoreAccess,
      [UserEmail] = USERPRINCIPALNAME()
      && [Role] = "Director"
    ),
    "RID", [RegionID]
  )
recommendedSolutions.examNote: The IN + SELECTCOLUMNS(FILTER(...)) pattern is more reliable than LOOKUPVALUE for multi-row RLS scenarios. LOOKUPVALUE returns only the FIRST match — if a regional director manages 30 stores and LOOKUPVALUE is used, they would only see one store's data.

title: Tailspin Toys Global Distribution
scenario: Tailspin Toys is a global toy manufacturer and distributor operating in 22 countries. Their Power BI solution serves 800 users including country managers, category leads, and a global supply chain team. The solution was built 18 months ago and is showing significant performance and governance issues as the business has scaled.
currentSetup: The model imports data from three sources: Azure SQL (global orders, 140M rows), Azure Blob Storage (product master CSV files, refreshed ad-hoc by the product team), and a third-party logistics API (delivery status, JSON format, updated every 6 hours). The model has 14 measures, 31 calculated columns on the FactOrders table, and 6 bidirectional relationships. Workspace: shared Premium P1 capacity. Users report 8–15 second load times. The product CSV files occasionally have schema changes (new columns added) that break the refresh pipeline. Country managers have raised concerns that they sometimes see order data from other countries.
requirements: Reduce average report load time to under 4 seconds
Prevent CSV schema changes from breaking the refresh pipeline
Ensure country managers see only their country's orders — investigate and fix the data leakage
Allow the product team to update product master data without IT involvement

questions.question: Performance Analyzer shows the FactOrders table accounts for 73% of model memory. The table has 140M rows, 31 calculated columns, and 6 bidirectional relationships. A DAX query on a top-10 country revenue visual takes 11 seconds. Which combination of changes will MOST effectively reduce model size and query time?
choices: Convert calculated columns that are used only in visuals (not in relationships or other measures) to measures; remove bidirectional relationships where single-direction filtering is sufficient; verify column data types are minimal (Integer vs Text for ID columns)
Switch FactOrders to DirectQuery mode to eliminate in-memory storage; this moves calculation to the Azure SQL engine which is optimized for 140M-row aggregation
Add aggregation tables in Power Query that pre-aggregate FactOrders to Country-Month grain; load both the aggregation table and detail table, configuring the aggregation table as a dual-storage model
Reduce the import date range from all history to the last 24 months using a query parameter; archive older data in a separate historical model
questions.explanation: Calculated columns are stored in memory per row — 31 columns on a 140M-row table creates massive VertiPaq pressure and causes slow compression scans. Converting display-only calculated columns to measures eliminates this overhead (measures compute at query time on aggregated data, not row-by-row). Bidirectional relationships force both-direction filter propagation which multiplies query complexity — removing unnecessary bidirectional filters significantly reduces DAX query plan branching. Correct data types (Integer IDs vs Text) dramatically improve VertiPaq dictionary compression. DirectQuery (B) eliminates in-memory storage but introduces network round-trips and typically increases, not decreases, load time for aggregation-heavy executive dashboards.

questions.question: The product team uploads updated product master CSV files to Azure Blob Storage. When the product team adds new columns to the CSV (e.g., a new 'EcoRating' attribute), the Power Query step that selects specific columns fails because the step references columns by name using Table.SelectColumns with a hardcoded list. The refresh pipeline errors with 'column not found'. What is the MOST resilient fix?
choices: Replace the Table.SelectColumns step with Table.SelectColumns that dynamically builds the column list using only columns confirmed to exist: Table.SelectColumns(Source, List.Intersect({requiredCols}, Table.ColumnNames(Source)))
Add a try/otherwise expression around the Table.SelectColumns step to silently ignore column errors and return the last successful refresh result
Set the CSV source query to use schema-on-read inference disabled so Power Query accepts any schema without validation
Create a Power Query parameter 'CSVSchema' that the product team updates manually each time they change the CSV structure before triggering refresh
questions.explanation: The root cause is a brittle column selection step that assumes a fixed schema. The resilient fix is to intersect the required column list with the actual column names available in the source — Table.SelectColumns only requests columns that exist. This allows the product team to add new columns to the CSV without breaking the pipeline; the Power Query step simply ignores columns it doesn't need. try/otherwise (B) would mask legitimate errors and could serve stale data silently — dangerous for a production pipeline. Schema-on-read disabling (C) is not a configurable option in this way. A manual parameter (D) defeats the goal of IT-free product team updates and is error-prone.

questions.question: Country managers report seeing order data from other countries. The model has a 'CountryManager' RLS role with filter on DimCountry: [CountryCode] = USERPRINCIPALNAME(). Investigation shows FactOrders has a bidirectional relationship with DimProduct, and DimProduct has an active relationship with a PromotionFact table. Promotions reference orders from multiple countries. What is the MOST likely cause of the data leakage and the correct fix?
choices: Bidirectional cross-filtering on the FactOrders ↔ DimProduct relationship allows filter context to propagate from PromotionFact through DimProduct back into FactOrders, bypassing the DimCountry RLS filter. Fix: change the FactOrders ↔ DimProduct relationship to single-direction (DimProduct → FactOrders).

The RLS filter [CountryCode] = USERPRINCIPALNAME() is comparing a country code (e.g., 'US') against an email UPN — the comparison always evaluates to FALSE for all users, so no filter is applied and all rows are visible.
The 'CountryManager' role has not been assigned to users in the Power BI Service — unassigned roles do not restrict access and default to showing all data.
DimCountry uses a text CountryCode column but FactOrders stores a numeric CountryID — the relationship is on mismatched data types, so the filter does not propagate correctly.
questions.explanation: This is a classic bidirectional relationship RLS leakage scenario. With bidirectional cross-filter on FactOrders ↔ DimProduct, filter context can flow FROM FactOrders TO DimProduct AND back. When PromotionFact is filtered, it can pull DimProduct rows from other countries' orders, and the bidirectional relationship then exposes those FactOrders rows — bypassing the DimCountry RLS filter that only directly filters DimCountry, not FactOrders through this cross-filter path. The fix is to revert to single-direction filtering where possible and use CROSSFILTER(FactOrders[ProductID], DimProduct[ProductID], NONE) in measures that need the reverse direction. Option B is plausible but if the filter always returned FALSE, NO data would be visible — the symptom is too much data, not too little.

recommendedSolutions.title: Product Team Self-Service via Blob Storage Access
recommendedSolutions.overview: Q2 makes the pipeline resilient to schema changes. This solution covers the access and process configuration so the product team can upload updated CSVs directly without involving IT or the BI team.

steps.label: Grant Blob Storage write access to product team
steps.detail: In Azure Portal, assign product team members the Storage Blob Data Contributor role on the specific container holding product master CSVs. They can upload files without accessing other infrastructure.

steps.label: Standardise the filename convention
steps.detail: Agree on a fixed filename (e.g., products_master.csv) so the Power Query source always points to the same path. The product team overwrites this file each time — they never change the path or filename.

steps.label: Provide a user-friendly upload interface
steps.detail: If the product team is non-technical, configure Azure Storage Explorer with a saved connection, or sync the container to a SharePoint document library. This gives them a familiar drag-and-drop interface without needing Azure Portal access.

steps.label: Schedule automatic refresh after upload window
steps.detail: Set the Power BI semantic model to refresh daily after the product team typical upload time. Optionally, configure an Azure Event Grid trigger connected to a Logic App that calls the Power BI REST API to refresh the model automatically when a new file is detected in the container.

recommendedSolutions.examNote: PL-300 exam tip: self-service data update requirements are solved by granting write access to the data source (SharePoint, OneDrive, Blob Storage) and making the Power Query pipeline schema-resilient. The List.Intersect fix from Q2 means the product team can safely add CSV columns without breaking the pipeline.

title: Lucerne E-Commerce Customer Analytics
scenario: Lucerne Publishing has transitioned from a physical book distributor to a digital e-commerce retailer. They sell e-books, audiobooks, and print-on-demand titles through their website and a marketplace channel. Their data team needs to build a Power BI solution for the marketing and product teams to analyse customer acquisition, conversion funnels, cart abandonment, and revenue attribution.
currentSetup: Data sources: (1) An Azure SQL Database containing FactOrders (2.8M rows, 3 years history) and DimCustomers, (2) a Google Analytics 4 export to BigQuery containing 140M web session and event rows in nested JSON format, (3) a flat CSV of marketing campaign spend from the media agency updated weekly. Orders contain a CustomerKey, OrderDate, Channel ('Direct', 'Marketplace'), ProductKey, Revenue, and DiscountPct. There is no session-to-order linkage in the current data model — marketing cannot determine which campaign drove each order.
requirements: Build a conversion funnel from session → product view → add-to-cart → purchase that updates weekly
Attribute revenue to the last marketing campaign the customer clicked before purchasing (last-click attribution model)
Allow the marketing team to analyse customer lifetime value (CLV) by cohort month and acquisition channel
The marketing manager must not see individual customer names or emails — only aggregated segment data

questions.subtopic: Convert semi-structured data to a table
questions.question: The Google Analytics 4 export in BigQuery stores event parameters as a repeated RECORD (nested JSON array). When the data analyst connects to BigQuery from Power Query, the event_params column appears as a [List] of [Record] objects. Each record has keys 'key' and 'value.string_value'. The analyst needs a column containing only the value where key = 'page_location'. Which Power Query transformation correctly extracts this?
choices: Add a custom column: = Table.SelectRows([event_params], each [key] = "page_location"){0}[value.string_value], then expand the resulting column
Right-click the event_params column and choose Expand to New Rows, then filter the key column for 'page_location' and pivot on the value column
Add a custom column using: = List.First(List.Select([event_params], each _[key] = "page_location"), null)?[value.string_value], then promote it
Use Table.TransformColumns to apply Text.FromBinary to the event_params column, then use JSON.Document to re-parse each row
questions.explanation: Option C uses List.Select to filter the nested list to matching records, List.First to safely get the first match (returning null if not found), and the ?[] null-safe accessor to extract the field. This pattern is robust when a session may not have the target event parameter. Option A would error when no matching row exists in the list. Option B (expand + filter + pivot) is valid but inefficient at 140M rows — it creates enormous intermediate tables before reducing. Option D applies Text transformation to structured data types, which would error or produce '[List]' string representation.

questions.subtopic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.question: The marketing team needs a [Customer Lifetime Value] measure showing total revenue per customer since their first order. They also want to slice by acquisition channel and cohort month (the month of the customer's first ever order). The model has FactOrders linked to DimCustomers (1:M) and DimDate linked to FactOrders on OrderDate. DimCustomers has a FirstOrderDate column and AcquisitionChannel. Which measure definition is MOST correct for CLV?
choices: Customer LTV = CALCULATE(SUM(FactOrders[Revenue]), ALL(DimDate))
Customer LTV = SUMX(VALUES(DimCustomers[CustomerKey]), CALCULATE(SUM(FactOrders[Revenue])))
Customer LTV = CALCULATE(SUM(FactOrders[Revenue]), REMOVEFILTERS(DimDate[Date]))
Customer LTV = DIVIDE(SUM(FactOrders[Revenue]), DISTINCTCOUNT(FactOrders[CustomerKey]))
questions.explanation: CLV should sum all revenue per customer regardless of any date slicer in the report — but respect customer-level filters (channel, cohort). SUMX over VALUES(CustomerKey) iterates each customer in the current filter context and CALCULATE within it sums that customer's total revenue without date restriction. Option A uses ALL(DimDate) which removes date filters globally but is a table-level function applied at measure level — this correctly removes date context but doesn't iterate per-customer correctly. Option C (REMOVEFILTERS on a single column) is similar to A but only removes the Date column filter, not filters on year/month slicers. Option D calculates average revenue per customer — not lifetime value.

questions.question: The product team wants a conversion funnel visual showing four stages: Sessions → Product Views → Add to Cart → Purchase. Each stage should display the count and the drop-off percentage from the previous stage. The stages are stored as separate measures: [Sessions], [ProductViews], [AddToCart], [Purchases]. Which built-in Power BI visual BEST represents this scenario?
choices: Stacked bar chart with stages on the Y-axis and count on the X-axis, formatted with data labels
Funnel chart with the four stage measures as values, sorted descending
Waterfall chart showing the decremental change between each funnel stage
Line chart with stages on the X-axis to show sequential progression
questions.explanation: The Funnel chart is designed precisely for sequential stage analysis — it renders stages as proportional horizontal bars narrowing toward the bottom, making drop-off immediately visible. It natively supports value labels showing count and percentage of first stage. A stacked bar chart (A) shows parts-of-a-whole within categories, not sequential narrowing — it would require manual workarounds and loses the funnel metaphor. A waterfall chart (C) shows incremental additions/subtractions, not proportional stage flow. A line chart (D) implies continuous trend over time rather than discrete conversion stages.

questions.question: The marketing manager must analyse campaign performance without being able to see individual customer names, email addresses, or phone numbers stored in DimCustomers. The marketing manager is a Member of the Marketing workspace. The current report shows a Customer Detail table visual with all DimCustomers columns. What is the MOST appropriate solution?
choices: Create an RLS role that filters DimCustomers to rows where [CustomerSegment] IS NOT NULL, excluding rows with personal identifiers
Remove the CustomerName, Email, and Phone columns from the semantic model in Power BI Desktop before publishing
Apply a sensitivity label marked 'Confidential' to the semantic model — this restricts column-level access for non-admin users
Grant the marketing manager Viewer access to the workspace instead of Member access to limit data visibility
questions.explanation: Removing PII columns from the semantic model at publish time is the most effective and lowest-maintenance solution. If the columns don't exist in the published model, they cannot be accessed by any report or direct query — regardless of workspace role. RLS (A) operates at the row level, not the column level, and cannot hide specific columns from a role while showing the rest of the row. Sensitivity labels (C) control export and sharing policies but do not enforce column-level access in reports — the data remains visible in the visual. Workspace roles (D) control whether a user can edit or share content, not which data columns they can see within a report.

recommendedSolutions.title: Last-Click Attribution Model in Power Query
recommendedSolutions.overview: Implement last-click attribution by joining campaign click data to orders based on the most recent click before each order date per customer.

steps.label: Prepare campaign click data
steps.detail: In Power Query, load the campaign click log (CustomerKey, CampaignName, ClickDateTime). Sort descending by ClickDateTime per customer so the most recent click appears first.

steps.label: Merge clicks to orders
steps.detail: From FactOrders, merge with the campaign clicks table using a left outer join on CustomerKey. Use Table.SelectRows within a custom column to find the latest click where ClickDateTime <= OrderDate for that customer.

steps.label: Extract attributing campaign
steps.detail: After the merge, expand only the CampaignName column. Null values indicate orders with no prior click (organic/direct). Add AttributedChannel = if CampaignName = null then 'Direct' else CampaignName.

recommendedSolutions.examNote: Last-click attribution is a data preparation problem, not a DAX problem. The correct answer is always to resolve attribution during ETL/Power Query so the model contains a single AttributedCampaign column per order — not to use complex CALCULATE logic per visual.

title: WingTip Toys HR Workforce Analytics
scenario: WingTip Toys is a consumer goods company with 4,200 employees across 9 countries. The People Analytics team is building a Power BI solution for HR Business Partners (HRBPs) and senior leadership to track headcount, attrition, hiring velocity, and workforce diversity. The solution must comply with regional data privacy regulations — European HRBPs must not see North American employee records, and vice versa.
currentSetup: Source data: an Azure SQL Database updated nightly containing DimEmployee (active and terminated employees, 4,200+ rows), FactHeadcountSnapshot (one row per employee per month-end, 12 months history), FactAttrition (all terminations with ReasonCode), and FactHires (all new hires with SourceChannel). HRBPs are mapped to regions in a BridgeHRBPRegion table that has columns HRBPEmail and Region. Each employee has a Region column. The current report shows a global headcount table with employee names, salaries, and performance ratings visible to all HRBPs.
requirements: HRBPs must only see employees in their assigned region — enforced server-side, not through report filtering
Leadership requires a headcount trend visual showing net headcount change month-over-month across all regions
The attrition rate measure must calculate correctly whether sliced by region, department, or job level
Time-to-fill (average days between position open date and hire date) must reflect only filled positions, not open requisitions

questions.question: HRBPs must be restricted to their assigned region's employee data. The BridgeHRBPRegion table maps HRBPEmail to Region. DimEmployee has a Region column. The two tables have no direct relationship — they are joined conceptually through region name. What is the MOST reliable RLS implementation?
choices: Create an RLS role with the filter on DimEmployee: [Region] = LOOKUPVALUE(BridgeHRBPRegion[Region], BridgeHRBPRegion[HRBPEmail], USERPRINCIPALNAME())
Create an RLS role that uses PATHCONTAINS to traverse the employee hierarchy and return only direct reports of the HRBP
Use a workspace role-based security policy that assigns each HRBP to a separate workspace containing only their region's app
Add a calculated column to DimEmployee: IsMyRegion = IF(USERPRINCIPALNAME() = LOOKUPVALUE(...), 1, 0) and filter the RLS role on IsMyRegion = 1
questions.explanation: LOOKUPVALUE inside an RLS DAX expression is the standard pattern for dynamic RLS when the user-to-data mapping is stored in a separate table without a model relationship. It returns the Region value for the currently authenticated user from BridgeHRBPRegion, and that value is compared to DimEmployee[Region] to filter visible rows. PATHCONTAINS (B) is for parent-child hierarchies (org charts), not region security. Workspace-per-region (C) is a distribution strategy, not security enforcement — determined users can still extract data. Calculated columns (D) evaluated at publish time cannot use USERPRINCIPALNAME() dynamically at runtime — the column value is fixed when the model is refreshed.

questions.subtopic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.question: The People Analytics team wants an [Attrition Rate] measure showing the percentage of employees who left during the selected period. The formula is: Terminations in period ÷ Average headcount in period. FactAttrition contains one row per termination with TerminationDate. FactHeadcountSnapshot has one row per employee per MonthEnd date. The measure must work correctly when sliced by Region, Department, or JobLevel. Which implementation is MOST correct?
choices: Attrition Rate = DIVIDE(COUNTROWS(FactAttrition), AVERAGEX(VALUES(DimDate[MonthEnd]), CALCULATE(COUNTROWS(FactHeadcountSnapshot))))
Attrition Rate = DIVIDE(COUNT(FactAttrition[TerminationDate]), COUNT(FactHeadcountSnapshot[EmployeeKey]))
Attrition Rate = DIVIDE(DISTINCTCOUNT(FactAttrition[EmployeeKey]), CALCULATE(DISTINCTCOUNT(FactHeadcountSnapshot[EmployeeKey]), ALL(DimDate)))
Attrition Rate = [Total Terminations] / [Opening Headcount]
questions.explanation: Option A correctly calculates average headcount by iterating over each MonthEnd value in the current date filter context using AVERAGEX and counts snapshot rows per month. This respects any Region/Department/JobLevel filter applied to the visual because those filters propagate through the relationships. Option B uses COUNT which counts non-blank values — it counts all snapshots (one per employee per month) rather than per-month averages. Option C uses ALL(DimDate) which removes the date filter completely from the denominator — this produces an average headcount across all history regardless of the selected period. Option D uses Opening Headcount as denominator instead of average, which is a different (less accurate) formula and introduces ambiguity when the period spans multiple months.

questions.subtopic: Identify use cases for calculated columns and calculated tables
questions.question: The team needs a [Time to Fill] measure that calculates the average number of days between a position's open date and hire date, but only for positions that have been filled (FactHires has a HireDate). Open requisitions have no HireDate and should be excluded. FactHires contains: RequisitionKey, OpenDate, HireDate (nullable), SourceChannel. Which approach is MOST appropriate?
choices: Create a calculated column in FactHires: DaysToFill = DATEDIFF([OpenDate], [HireDate], DAY), then create a measure: Time to Fill = AVERAGE(FactHires[DaysToFill])
Create a measure: Time to Fill = AVERAGEX(FILTER(FactHires, NOT ISBLANK(FactHires[HireDate])), DATEDIFF(FactHires[OpenDate], FactHires[HireDate], DAY))
Create a measure: Time to Fill = DIVIDE(SUMX(FactHires, DATEDIFF([OpenDate], [HireDate], DAY)), COUNTROWS(FactHires))
Add a calculated column IsFilled = IF(ISBLANK([HireDate]), 0, 1) then measure: Time to Fill = CALCULATE(AVERAGE(FactHires[DaysToFill]), FactHires[IsFilled] = 1)
questions.explanation: Option B is correct: AVERAGEX with FILTER(FILTER handles the null exclusion dynamically, and DATEDIFF computes the duration per row within the iterator. This respects any report filters (SourceChannel, region, etc.) applied to the visual. Option A (calculated column) works but has a flaw: AVERAGE of a column that contains blank values from open requisitions will still include those rows in Power BI's column average unless explicitly filtered — calculated columns containing BLANK are excluded from aggregation, so actually A would work, but B is more explicit and filter-context-aware. Option C divides by COUNTROWS(FactHires) which includes open requisitions in the denominator — producing a lower average than correct. Option D requires maintaining two calculated columns and is unnecessarily complex.

questions.subtopic: Enhance reports for usability and storytelling
questions.question: Senior leadership wants a headcount trend showing net change month-over-month (MoM) across all regions. The visual should make it immediately obvious which months had net headcount growth (more hires than attrition) vs net decline. The data is available as measures [Hires], [Terminations], and [Net Change] = Hires - Terminations by month. Which visual and configuration BEST meets this requirement?
choices: A line chart with [Net Change] on the Y-axis and MonthEnd on the X-axis, with a reference line at 0 and conditional coloring above/below the line
A waterfall chart with [Hires] as an increase value and [Terminations] as a decrease value by month, showing the running headcount balance
A clustered bar chart with [Hires] and [Terminations] as two series by month, with a secondary axis for [Net Change]
A matrix visual with months as rows and [Hires], [Terminations], [Net Change] as columns, formatted with conditional formatting on [Net Change]
questions.explanation: A line chart with a 0 reference line and conditional coloring is the clearest way to show signed net change — months above zero are positive (growth) and months below are negative (decline). The reference line creates an immediate visual anchor. In Power BI, you can use the line chart's analytics pane to add a constant line at 0. Option B (waterfall) is excellent for showing cumulative running totals but makes MoM change comparison harder across many months — it's better for YTD bridges. Option C uses two series which forces users to mentally subtract bars rather than showing the net signal directly. Option D (matrix) is a table — it requires reading numbers rather than visually identifying growth vs decline months.

recommendedSolutions.title: Dynamic RLS with Regional HRBP Mapping
recommendedSolutions.overview: Implement server-side row-level security using a bridging table that maps HRBP email to region, enforced through DAX USERPRINCIPALNAME().

steps.label: Create the RLS role in Power BI Desktop
steps.detail: In Power BI Desktop, go to Modeling → Manage Roles. Create a role named 'HRBP'. Apply a table filter to DimEmployee with the DAX expression: [Region] = LOOKUPVALUE(BridgeHRBPRegion[Region], BridgeHRBPRegion[HRBPEmail], USERPRINCIPALNAME()). This expression runs at query time, looking up the current user's email in the bridge table.

steps.label: Verify with View As
steps.detail: Use the 'View as role' feature in Desktop, specifying a test user email. Confirm that only employees in the mapped region appear. Test with a user who has multiple region mappings (if applicable) by checking that LOOKUPVALUE returns the correct single value — if one email maps to multiple regions, use a different pattern such as a disconnected security table with TREATAS.

steps.label: Assign users in Power BI Service
steps.detail: After publishing, navigate to the semantic model security settings. Add each HRBP's Azure AD account or security group to the 'HRBP' role. Leadership accounts requiring full visibility should NOT be added to the HRBP role — they see all data by default. RLS only applies to non-admin workspace members assigned to a role.

recommendedSolutions.examNote: USERPRINCIPALNAME() returns the authenticated user's email at query time — it cannot be used in calculated columns (evaluated at refresh time). Workspace admins and owners bypass RLS by default — this is a known PL-300 exam trap. Assign all HRBPs as Viewers or Members, never as Admins, when RLS enforcement is required.
